title: Lexington & Ohio Railroad
summary: The Lexington and Ohio Railroad, the second-oldest rail line west of the Alleghenies, set out to link Lexington with Frankfort and the Ohio River.
bodyMarkdown:
On January 27, 1830, the Kentucky General Assembly chartered the Lexington and Ohio Railroad. It was the first railroad in Kentucky and the [second-oldest railroad line west of the Allegheny Mountains](https://grokipedia.com/page/louisville,_cincinnati_and_lexington_railway). Its job was to build a line west from Lexington to the Ohio River.

## A route to world markets

[ExploreKYHistory explains](https://explorekyhistory.ky.gov/items/show/509) that the backers wanted a commercial line from Lexington to the river. From there, goods could travel by water to New Orleans and on to markets around the world. Plans called for the line to follow the watershed of Elkhorn Creek toward Frankfort.

The first rail was laid with a ceremony on October 22, 1831. By October 1832 the company had about 2 miles of track. In June 1833 the line reached the halfway point between Lexington and Frankfort, which later gave rise to the town of Midway.

## Stone sills and strap iron

The L&O did not use the raised rails of later railroads. Its track was made of limestone blocks topped with flat iron straps imported from England. Horses pulled the first cars. A steam engine built in Lexington in 1833 failed, so two engines were brought in from the East Coast.

The line reached Frankfort on January 30, 1834, but stopped on a bluff above the city. Cars used a 2,200-foot incline to get down into the valley. In 1835 the engine "Daniel Boone" made the trip of almost 29 miles from Lexington to Frankfort in two hours and twenty-nine minutes. Its arrival in the [capital](/stories/frankfort-franks-ford-becomes-the-capital/) was celebrated with cannon fire and a ball at the Weisiger House hotel.

## Debt and state ownership

The strap-iron rails soon wore out and caused several accidents. They were later replaced with wooden ties and standard T-rails. Money was also a problem. By 1837 the company had no cash, and by 1840 it was insolvent.

On January 12, 1842, the railroad was sold at public auction in Frankfort, and the state bought it for over $178,000. A tunnel later took the line into downtown Frankfort. In 1848 a new Lexington and Frankfort Railroad, owned partly by the state and the city of Lexington, took over the line.

## Toward Louisville and the L&N

ExploreKYHistory says the extension to Louisville was finished in 1851, when the railroad bridge over the Kentucky River was built. When the [Louisville and Nashville Railroad](/stories/louisville-nashville-railroad-opens-the-interior/) was completed in 1859, Bluegrass farmers gained a rail link to southern markets. During the Civil War, raids by both sides destroyed much of what had been built.

The line later became part of the Louisville, Cincinnati and Lexington Railway. The L&N bought that company on July 1, 1881.

## Kentucky today

Historical Marker #69 in Frankfort remembers the Lexington and Ohio. Much of today's track covers the same ground, and the old rights-of-way now form parts of the CSX system. Midway, the town that grew up on the line, still sits between Lexington and Frankfort.
